title: No. 46 — The Influence of the State and Federal Governments Compared (Madison)
paragraphs: RESUMING the subject of the last paper, I now turn to the question of whether the federal or the State governments will have the advantage in the people's preference and support. Despite the different ways they are appointed, we must regard both as substantially dependent on the great body of the citizens of the United States. I take this as given here regarding the federal government, reserving the proofs for another place. The federal and State governments are in fact different agents and trustees of the people, set up with different powers and designed for different purposes. The opponents of the Constitution seem to have lost sight of the people altogether in their reasoning on this subject. They have viewed these different establishments not only as mutual rivals and enemies, but as if no common authority above them controlled their attempts to seize each other's powers. These gentlemen need to be reminded of their error. They must be told that the ultimate authority, wherever derivative authority may sit, resides in the people alone. Whether either or which of these governments will be able to expand its sphere of jurisdiction at the other's expense will not depend merely on the comparative ambition or skill of those governments. Truth, no less than decency, requires that we suppose the outcome in every case to depend on the views and approval of their common constituents.

Many considerations, beyond those raised earlier, seem to put it beyond doubt that the people's first and most natural attachment will be to the governments of their respective States. Into State administration, a greater number of individuals will hope to rise. From State patronage, a greater number of offices and salaries will flow. By State oversight, the more domestic and personal interests of the people will be regulated and provided for. With State affairs, the people will be more familiar and minutely acquainted. And with State officials, a greater proportion of the people will share ties of personal acquaintance, friendship, and family or party loyalty. So the popular bias may well be expected to lean most strongly to that side.

Experience tells the same story. The federal administration, even though far less developed than what may be hoped under a better system, had during the war, and especially while the independent paper money was still trusted, an activity and importance as great as it could have under any future circumstances. It was also engaged in a course of measures aimed at protecting everything that was dear to the people and acquiring everything that was desirable. Yet it was consistently found that, after the brief enthusiasm for the early Congresses had passed, the people's attention and attachment turned back to their own State governments. The federal council was never the idol of popular favor, and opposition to proposed enlargements of its powers and importance was the standard position taken by men who hoped to build their political careers on the prepossessions of their fellow-citizens.

If, therefore, as has been remarked elsewhere, the people in future come to favor the federal over the State governments, the change can only result from such clear and irresistible proof of better administration that it overcomes all their prior leanings. In that case, the people surely should not be barred from giving most of their confidence where they find it most deserved. But even then, the State governments would have little to fear, because the federal power can, by its nature, be advantageously administered only within a certain sphere.
The remaining points on which I propose to compare the federal and State governments are the disposition and the ability that each may possess to resist and frustrate the measures of the other.

It has already been proved that members of the federal government will be more dependent on members of the State governments than the State officials will be on the federal. It has also appeared that the prepossessions of the people, on whom both depend, will lean more toward the State governments than the federal. So far as each government's disposition toward the other is shaped by these causes, the State governments must clearly have the advantage. But in another distinct and very important way, the advantage will lie on the same side. The prepossessions that members will themselves carry into the federal government will generally favor the States, while it will rarely happen that members of the State governments carry into their public councils a bias in favor of the general government. A local spirit will inevitably prevail much more in the members of Congress than a national spirit will prevail in the State legislatures. Everyone knows that a great proportion of the errors made by State legislatures comes from the members' tendency to sacrifice the broad and lasting interests of the State to the particular and separate views of the counties or districts where they live. And if they cannot widen their thinking enough to embrace the collective welfare of their own State, how can we imagine they will make the aggregate prosperity of the Union, and the dignity and respectability of its government, the objects of their affection and deliberation? For the same reason that members of the State legislatures will not adequately attach themselves to national objects, members of the federal legislature will likely attach themselves too much to local ones. The States will be to federal members what counties and towns are to State members. Measures will too often be decided by their probable effect not on national prosperity and happiness, but on the prejudices, interests, and pursuits of the governments and people of individual States. What is the spirit that has generally characterized the proceedings of Congress? A reading of their journals, and the candid admissions of those who have served in that assembly, will tell us that the members have too often acted as partisans of their respective States rather than as impartial guardians of a common interest. Where on one occasion improper sacrifices have been made of local concerns to enlarge the federal government, the great interests of the nation have suffered on a hundred occasions from undue attention to the local prejudices, interests, and views of the particular States. I do not mean by these reflections to suggest that the new federal government will not embrace a broader plan of policy than the existing government has pursued, much less that its views will be as confined as those of the State legislatures. I mean only that it will share enough of the spirit of both to be reluctant to invade the rights of the individual States or the prerogatives of their governments. The motives of the State governments to expand their prerogatives at the expense of the federal will not be matched by any reciprocal predisposition in the federal members.

Even if we were to grant that the federal government may feel an equal disposition with the State governments to push its power beyond proper limits, the States would still have the advantage in the means of defeating such encroachments. If an act of a particular State, though hostile to the national government, is generally popular in that State and does not too grossly violate the oaths of State officers, it is carried out immediately, by means on the spot, and depending on the State alone. The opposition of the federal government, or the intervention of federal officers, would only inflame the zeal of all parties on the State's side. The evil could not be prevented or repaired, if at all, without the use of means that must always be resorted to with reluctance and difficulty. On the other hand, if a federal measure is unpopular in particular States, which would seldom fail to be the case if the measure were unwarrantable and may sometimes happen even when the measure is warranted, the means of opposition are powerful and ready at hand. The unease of the people, their reluctance and perhaps refusal to cooperate with federal officers, the disapproval of the State executive, and the embarrassments created by legislative maneuvers that would often be added on such occasions, would create difficulties in any State that should not be underestimated. In a large State, they would form very serious obstacles. And where several adjoining States happened to share the same view, they would present obstructions the federal government would scarcely be willing to confront.

But ambitious encroachments by the federal government on the authority of the State governments would not provoke the opposition of just a single State, or of only a few. They would be signals of general alarm. Every State government would take up the common cause. Correspondence would be opened. Plans of resistance would be coordinated. One spirit would animate and direct the whole. The same combinations, in short, would result from fear of federal tyranny as were produced by the dread of a foreign yoke. And unless the proposed innovations were voluntarily abandoned, the same appeal to a trial of force would be made in this case as was made in the other. But what kind of madness could ever push the federal government to such an extreme? In the contest with Great Britain, one part of the empire was used against another. The more numerous part invaded the rights of the less numerous part. The attempt was unjust and unwise, but it was not in theory absolutely impossible. But what would be the contest in the case we are imagining? Who would be the parties? A few representatives of the people would be opposed to the people themselves, or rather one set of representatives would be contending against thirteen sets of representatives, with the whole body of their common constituents on the side of the latter.

The only refuge left for those who predict the downfall of the State governments is the fanciful supposition that the federal government may first build up a military force for the projects of ambition. The reasonings in these papers must have been employed to little purpose if it is now necessary to disprove the reality of this danger. To suppose that the people and the States would, for a long enough period, elect an unbroken succession of men ready to betray both. That the traitors would, throughout that period, uniformly and systematically pursue some fixed plan to expand the military establishment. That the State governments and people would silently and patiently watch the gathering storm and continue to supply its materials until it was ready to burst on their own heads. All this must seem to anyone more like the incoherent dreams of a delirious jealousy, or the misjudged exaggerations of fake zeal, than the sober concerns of genuine patriotism. Extravagant as the supposition is, let us make it anyway. Let a regular army, fully matching the country's resources, be formed and entirely devoted to the federal government. Even then, it would not be too much to say that the State governments, with the people on their side, would be able to repel the danger. According to the best estimates, the highest size a standing army can reach in any country is about one hundredth of the population, or one twenty-fifth of those able to bear arms. In the United States, that proportion would yield an army of no more than twenty-five or thirty thousand men. Against them would stand a militia of nearly half a million citizens armed and ready, officered by men chosen from among themselves, fighting for their common liberties, and united and led by governments that hold their affections and confidence. It may well be doubted whether a militia in this position could ever be defeated by such a small proportion of regular troops. Those most familiar with the recent successful resistance of this country against the British will be the most inclined to deny the possibility. Beyond the advantage of being armed, which Americans hold over the people of almost every other nation, the existence of subordinate governments to which the people are attached, and which appoint the militia officers, forms a barrier against the schemes of ambition more impassable than any a simple government of any form can offer. Despite the military establishments in the various kingdoms of Europe, which are pushed as far as public resources will bear, the governments are afraid to trust their people with arms. And it is uncertain whether even with arms alone the people would not be able to throw off their yokes. But if the people had the further advantage of local governments chosen by themselves, that could gather the national will and direct the national force, and of officers appointed from the militia by these governments, attached both to them and to the militia, it can be said with the greatest confidence that the throne of every tyranny in Europe would soon be overturned in spite of the legions surrounding it. Let us not insult the free and gallant citizens of America with the suspicion that they would be less able to defend rights they actually possess than the degraded subjects of arbitrary power would be to wrest theirs from their oppressors. Let us rather no longer insult them with the supposition that they could ever reduce themselves to the necessity of making the experiment, by blindly and tamely submitting to the long train of insidious measures that must precede and produce it.

The argument under this heading can be put in a very compact form, and it appears entirely conclusive. Either the way the federal government is to be constructed will make it sufficiently dependent on the people, or it will not. On the first supposition, that dependence will keep it from forming schemes offensive to its constituents. On the other supposition, it will not have the people's confidence, and its schemes of usurpation will be easily defeated by the State governments, who will be backed by the people.

Summing up the considerations stated in this paper and the last, they amount to the most convincing evidence that the powers proposed for the federal government are as little dangerous to those reserved to the individual States as they are absolutely necessary to accomplish the purposes of the Union. And all the alarms sounded about a planned and consequent annihilation of the State governments must, on the most charitable reading, be ascribed to the chimerical fears of those who raise them.
